name: JoAnna Mendoza
bio: JoAnna Mendoza grew up in a farmworker family in Pinal County and served 20 years in the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, including as a drill instructor and on deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan. She later worked as a nonprofit leader, veterans advocate and congressional staffer, and holds a master's degree in leadership from Grand Canyon University. She is the Democratic nominee for Arizona's 6th district.

platform.point: Crack down on price gouging, modernize the Child Tax Credit and oppose tariffs she says raise prices.
Opposes benefit cuts and supports exploring ways to raise Social Security benefits for seniors on fixed incomes.
Reverse cuts to AHCCCS and enhanced ACA subsidies, expand Medicare drug price negotiation and add vision, hearing and dental coverage.
Supports apprenticeships, technical education, small businesses and the right to unionize.
Pairs port-of-entry security and deporting violent criminals with legal pathways to citizenship and detention-facility oversight.
Protect local solar projects, require data centers to bring their own energy, and secure Arizona's Colorado River share.
Backs NATO and diplomacy, and wants congressional approval before U.S. troops enter new conflicts.
Supports banning members of Congress and top officials from trading individual stocks.

economy.evidence: Wants to crack down on price gouging, have the wealthiest pay their fair share, close corporate loopholes and oppose tariffs.

welfare.evidence: Wants to reverse AHCCCS and ACA subsidy cuts, add dental, vision and hearing to Medicare, and in the 2026 debate called new SNAP work requirements barriers.

liberty.evidence: Abortion only: opposed a proposed VA abortion ban, saying people should be able to make their own health decisions.

security.evidence: Supports police funding, training and body cameras and opposes cutting police budgets, while also backing more crisis responders and transparency.

immigration.evidence: Supports legal pathways to citizenship, detention-facility oversight and the Stop Excessive Force in Immigration Act, plus port-of-entry security and deporting violent criminals.

foreign.evidence: Backs NATO, alliances and diplomacy but wants congressional approval before troops enter new conflicts and criticized the Iran war as lacking a plan.

energy.evidence: Supports clean-energy investment, protecting local solar projects and tackling climate change, while emphasizing lower utility costs.

education.evidence: General statement: pledges to expand access to education and supports workforce training and technical education.

notes: Read her campaign issue subpages, news releases and coverage of the September 2026 debate; several local outlets blocked automated access. No statements found on tech regulation or religion, and her gun policy is described only in general terms.

name: Daniel Butierez
bio: Daniel Butierez is a third-generation Arizonan who runs two businesses, including a painting contracting company, and has said he once experienced homelessness himself. He was the Republican nominee for Arizona's 7th district in 2024 and in the 2025 special election, and is the nominee again in 2026.

platform.point: Secure the southern border and give the U.S. Border Patrol the resources it needs.
Simplify the tax code toward a flatter system without the IRS, while closing loopholes for large corporations and the very wealthy.
Tie shelter access to mandatory drug rehabilitation and work requirements, and enforce anti-vagrancy laws.
Keep ICE as a law enforcement agency and pass the bipartisan Dignity Act to protect long-term residents from deportation.
Seeks federal funding for desalination, including a pipeline from the Sea of Cortez; data centers should build water treatment first.
Backs mining with safeguards and a mix of renewable energy and fossil fuels to lower costs.
Cut wasteful spending through bipartisan audits of federal programs and reform entitlement programs for long-term sustainability.
Opposes a federal role in education and supports school choice.

economy.evidence: Calls for a flatter tax code without the IRS, fewer regulations and faster permitting, though he also wants to close loopholes for the ultra-wealthy.

welfare.evidence: Proposes shelter access tied to mandatory rehab and work requirements, aid targeted to veterans and families, and entitlement reform.

liberty.evidence: Drug policy only: supports mandatory drug rehabilitation tied to shelter access and court-ordered treatment for severe mental illness.

security.evidence: Proposes enforcing anti-vagrancy laws and involving local law enforcement in homelessness interventions.

immigration.evidence: In 2025 backed a border wall and deporting recent unauthorized entrants; in 2026 defended ICE but urged passing the Dignity Act for long-term residents.

foreign.evidence: Said in a 2025 debate that he stands with Israel and supports continued assistance to Ukraine against Russia.

energy.evidence: General statement: backs expanding renewables alongside a balanced approach to fossil fuels, and supports mining for electric-vehicle minerals.

education.evidence: Opposed any federal role in education and praised school choice, including charter and private schools, in a 2025 debate.

faith.evidence: Wants federal funding redirected to treatment centers, including faith-based recovery programs.

notes: Used his campaign policy subpages plus coverage of the 2025 and August 2026 debates; the Arizona Daily Star and Tucson Sentinel blocked automated access. No statements found on tech regulation, and his liberty score rests on drug policy alone.

name: Peter Verbica
bio: Peter Coe Verbica is a San Jose native, a certified financial planner with a law degree, and a principal at the investment advisory firm Silicon Private Wealth; he previously taught as an adjunct at San Jose State University. He ran for the California Board of Equalization in 2022 and is the Republican nominee for California's 19th congressional district in 2026.

platform.point: Wants to end high gas taxes and California-specific fuel blend requirements.
Supports storage projects such as Sites Reservoir, desalination and recycling, and adjusting Endangered Species Act rules on water.
Link HUD funding to local zoning reform, convert federal surplus land to housing and streamline environmental review.
Proposes federal wildfire reinsurance or bond mechanisms and funding for grid hardening and forest fuel reduction.
Opposes PAGA lawsuits and limits on independent contractors, and backs tax incentives for reshoring manufacturing.
Favors insurance competition across state lines and price transparency over what he calls a government takeover.
Treat fentanyl supply as a national-security priority, with mandatory treatment for users and strict public-order laws.
Calls for immigration reform that serves the technology and farm sectors, alongside border security.

economy.evidence: Opposes PAGA litigation and independent-contractor rules, and wants lower income, sales and gas taxes.

welfare.evidence: Wants market-based health reform such as cross-state insurance competition and price transparency, and opposes a government takeover of health care.

liberty.evidence: Drug policy only: wants to discourage personal fentanyl possession through mandatory treatment and strict public-order laws.

security.evidence: Wants federal law enforcement and national-security tools used against trafficking networks and public order restored in cities.

immigration.evidence: General statement: pairs border security and interagency enforcement with immigration reform to help the tech and farm sectors.

foreign.evidence: Supports a strong national defense and stronger deterrence against China's military expansion.

energy.evidence: Wants to end gas taxes and California's special fuel blends and seek EPA waivers for more gasoline options, while also backing EV charging in low-income areas.

education.evidence: General statement: lists school choice among the policies he supports.

notes: Read his campaign site, the press releases linked from its news page and his iVoterGuide profile, where he answered no questions. No statements found on tech regulation, religion, abortion or guns.

name: Robin Littau
current_role: Enterprise Elementary School District board trustee
bio: Robin Littau is a Redding resident who served four years in the U.S. Coast Guard as a machinery technician. She owns a cleaning company and Joyful Living Magazine, and was elected to the Enterprise Elementary School District board in 2024. She is the Republican nominee for California's 2nd congressional district.

platform.point: Cut excessive regulation and require responsible federal spending.
Supports local control over decisions.
Wants to end border chaos and modernize citizenship requirements.
Supports a Parental Bill of Rights and opposes mandates under the slogan My Kid, My Call.
Supports law enforcement and stronger deterrents against predators.
Calls for fewer rules on small businesses.

economy.evidence: General statement: calls for cutting excessive regulation, fewer rules on small business and responsible spending.

security.evidence: General statement: lists supporting law enforcement and stronger deterrents among her priorities.

education.evidence: General statement: campaigns on a Parental Bill of Rights and parents deciding for their own children.

notes: Found her campaign site, which lists only short headings, and a 2024 school board Q&A with general answers. Her immigration headings were too vague to score, and no positions were found on welfare, abortion, guns, foreign policy, energy, tech or religion.

name: Sandra Van Scotter
current_role: Direct support professional and disability advocate
bio: Sandra Van Scotter is a former respiratory therapist who now works as a direct support professional for adults with developmental disabilities in Kern County. She advises the Kern Regional Center through its Self-Determination Program local advisory committee and has lived in Ridgecrest since 2014. This is her first campaign for office.

platform.point: Supports Medicare for All and a constitutional amendment making health care a right.
Opposes cuts to Medi-Cal in H.R. 1.
Pledges to advance access and inclusion for people with disabilities.
Promises town halls and direct office access for veterans and military families.
Backs border security plus legal status for long-settled undocumented workers, and says birthright citizenship should stand.
Supports sustainable water policy for farmers and help for rural towns with contaminated water.
Says higher earners should pay more to fund relief for working families.
Says the U.S. should not be at war in Iran and diplomacy should be restored.

economy.evidence: Strongly agreed that higher earners should pay more taxes to fund relief for working families.

welfare.evidence: Supports Medicare for All as a constitutional right and chose government-guaranteed universal health care with no private option.

liberty.evidence: Opposes abortion restrictions and Comstock Act enforcement and supports gender-affirming care and transgender inclusion, but backs red-flag laws and opposes military-style weapons.

immigration.evidence: Supports sanctuary cities, legal status for undocumented workers and birthright citizenship.

foreign.evidence: Said the U.S. is too involved abroad and should focus on its own sovereignty, and opposed the war in Iran.

energy.evidence: Named solar and wind as the most reliable sources for growing electricity demand.

tech.evidence: Said online platforms should bear financial and legal accountability for child sexual exploitation.

education.evidence: Strongly disagreed with eliminating the U.S. Department of Education, calling federal funding the main equalizer for under-resourced districts.

faith.evidence: Described church-state separation as barring government from favoring any faith and called civil marriage a legal function separate from religious definitions.

notes: Scores draw on her own answers to the iVoterGuide questionnaire, her campaign pages and 23ABC primary coverage; the KGET questionnaire blocked automated access. No clear statement was found on police or surveillance powers.

name: Tessa Lynn Hodge
bio: Tessa Lynn Hodge is a licensed clinical social worker who grew up in the High Desert region of California's 23rd District. She has worked as a medical social worker in local hospitals, with children in foster care and in school mental health services, and helped San Bernardino County put state and federal legislation into county policy. This is her first campaign for Congress.

platform.point: Fight for a single-payer health care system and train more health care workers.
Hold insurers accountable for covering therapy and expand training for mental health professionals.
Invest in a range of housing, from affordable rentals to pathways to homeownership.
Use federal legislation and infrastructure investment to bring skilled, well-paying jobs to the district.
Create a pathway to legal status for long-term residents and keep families together.
Supports stronger emission standards, federal clean-energy job funding and protecting public lands such as Joshua Tree.
Calls for a Gaza ceasefire, ending U.S. funding to Israel and repealing anti-BDS laws, and rebuilding ties with allies.
Opposes eliminating the Department of Education, citing its funding for rural schools.

economy.evidence: Wants federal legislation and infrastructure investment to bring skilled jobs to the district and criticizes insurance executives who profit by denying care.

welfare.evidence: Pledges to fight for a single-payer health care system covering everyone.

immigration.evidence: Supports a pathway to legal status for long-term residents, opposes deportations that split families and opposes a proposed local detention facility.

foreign.evidence: Wants to rebuild alliances and help other countries, but calls for ending U.S. funding to Israel and repealing anti-BDS laws.

energy.evidence: Pledges stronger emission standards and major federal funding for clean-energy jobs.

education.evidence: Says the Department of Education cannot be eliminated because its programs fund rural public schools.

notes: Read each campaign issue subpage, a Redlands candidate Q&A and BakersfieldNow coverage. No statements found on abortion, guns, policing, tech regulation or religion.

name: Joe Males
current_role: Hemet mayor pro tem and City Council member
bio: Joe Males is Hemet's mayor pro tem and represents District 4 on the city council. He is a Marine Corps veteran who left the service as a sergeant, and he founded a computer networking business in 1996. He ran for city council to focus on public safety after the murder of his son, also a Marine, which he discusses in his campaign biography.

platform.point: Make public safety and the rule of law a priority.
Reduce gas taxes and roll back regulations to lower costs for families.
Fight unnecessary regulations and bring manufacturing jobs back to the U.S.
Supports domestic energy production.
Calls for stronger border enforcement and following legal immigration processes.
As a council candidate, proposed a dedicated shelter building and hospital partnerships for mental health care.
Improve infrastructure and support business growth in the Inland Empire and Imperial County.
Support veterans, drawing on his roles with veterans' organizations.

economy.evidence: Calls for cutting gas taxes and rolling back regulations he says burden small businesses.

security.evidence: General statement: centers his campaign on public safety, the rule of law and fighting crime and gang violence.

immigration.evidence: General statement: emphasizes stronger border enforcement and following legal immigration processes.

energy.evidence: Backs domestic energy production and lower gas taxes to cut costs.

notes: His campaign site is a single page with no issues section; positions come from NBC Palm Springs and Desert Sun coverage and local council reporting. No statements found on health or welfare programs, social issues, foreign policy, tech, education or religion.

name: Jacqui Irwin
bio: Jacqui Irwin has served in the California State Assembly since 2014, first for the 44th District and since 2022 for the 42nd, and has chaired the Revenue and Taxation and the Military and Veterans Affairs committees. She previously served on the Thousand Oaks City Council and as mayor, and worked as a systems engineer at Teledyne and the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory. She holds a systems engineering degree from UC San Diego.

platform.point: Address the rising cost of living, including federal action to ease construction barriers and fund affordable housing.
Oppose what she describes as Trump's attacks on democracy and shared values.
Expand gun safety measures, building on her gun violence restraining order legislation.
Cites her work reauthorizing California's climate law.
Improve wildfire resilience and access to home insurance.
Protect access to health care.
Chairs the Assembly select committee on cybersecurity and wrote laws requiring security reviews of state agencies.
Authored laws expanding veterans' access to mental health treatment and consumer protections for active-duty service members.

liberty.evidence: Guns and LGBTQ rights: wrote laws letting gun violence restraining orders last up to five years, and passed legislation supporting LGBTQ seniors.

security.evidence: Wrote laws to help police investigate online crime and secured $3 million to help recover guns from people barred from owning them.

energy.evidence: Highlights her role in reauthorizing California's climate law and co-wrote recycled-plastic content requirements.

tech.evidence: Pushed AI companies to disclose training data and wrote the first security requirements for internet-connected devices.

education.evidence: Higher education only: secured state funding for a CSU Channel Islands engineering school and reformed community college placement policies.

photo.author: Master Sgt. David J. Loeffler, California National Guard

notes: Her campaign site has no issues page, and she answered no iVoterGuide questions; scores rest on her Assembly record from her biography and Wikipedia. The search limit was reached before her Assembly votes on taxes, health programs and immigration could be checked, so those topics remain unscored.
